# Press Release

Beam Therapeutics Reports Initial Clinical Data from Phase 1/2 Trial of BEAM-301, Demonstrating Proof of Concept for Genetic Correction in Glycogen Storage Disease Type Ia (GSDIa) at ESGCT 33rd Annual Congress

October 27, 2026 at 7:00 AM EDT

In the 40 mg Cohort, Two Patients Achieved 15 Hours of Controlled Fasting, Improvements in Glucose Control and No Longer Required Starch Supplementation Following Treatment 

Safety Profile of BEAM-301 Consistent with LNP-Based Therapies

Beam Plans to Engage FDA on Potential Path to Approval; Enrollment in 60 mg Dose Cohort Underway

Company to Host Investor Webcast Today, October 27, 2026, at 8:00 a.m. ET

CAMBRIDGE, Mass., Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Beam Therapeutics Inc. (Nasdaq: BEAM), a biotechnology company developing precision genetic medicines through base editing, today reported initial data from the ongoing Phase 1/2 clinical trial evaluating BEAM-301 for the treatment of glycogen storage disease type Ia (GSDIa). The data will be presented during a poster session at the 33^{rd} Annual Congress of the European Society of Gene and Cell Therapy (ESGCT) in Hamburg, Germany. BEAM-301 is an investigational liver-targeting lipid-nanoparticle (LNP) formulation of base editing reagents designed to correct the R83C mutation, one of the most prevalent disease-causing mutations in GSDIa and one that is associated with the most severe form of the disease.

“These findings demonstrate the potential for BEAM-301 to fundamentally change how patients with GSDIa manage their disease,” said Rebecca Riba-Wolman, M.D., director of the glycogen storage disease program and disorders of hypoglycemia at Connecticut Children’s and University of Connecticut School of Medicine, and presenting investigator in the BEAM-301 Phase 1/2 trial. “The ability of two patients to achieve 15 hours of controlled fasting and no longer require starch supplementation following a single treatment represents a significant departure from the intensive daily management typically required for this disease. While these are early results, the improvements in glucose regulation and reductions in starch requirements provide encouraging evidence of BEAM-301’s potential to deliver meaningful and lasting benefits for patients.”

BEAM-301 Phase 1/2 Clinical Trial Data Update
BEAM-301 is being evaluated in an open-label Phase 1/2 dose-exploration trial to investigate its safety, tolerability, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and efficacy in patients with GSDIa who are homozygous or compound heterozygous for the R83C variant. As of the August 17, 2026, data cutoff, six patients had received a single intravenous infusion of BEAM-301, including three patients treated with 20 mg and three patients treated with 40 mg. Median follow-up across both cohorts was 7.6 months (range: 1.9–16.6 months).

BEAM-301: In vivo LNP liver-targeting for GSDIa

BEAM-301 is a liver-targeting LNP formulation of base editing reagents designed to correct the R83C mutation, the most prevalent disease-causing mutation for, and the mutation which results in the most severe form of, GSDIa. GSDIa is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the G6PC gene that disrupts a key enzyme, G6Pase, critical for maintaining glucose homeostasis. Inhibition of G6Pase activity results in low fasting blood glucose levels that can result in seizures and be fatal. Patients with this mutation typically require ongoing corn starch administration, without which they may enter into hypoglycemic shock within one to three hours.

We are conducting a Phase 1/2 clinical trial of BEAM-301 at a select number of sites in the United States. The trial is an open-label, multi-cohort, single-ascending dose evaluation of BEAM-301 for the treatment of GSDIa in patients with the R83C mutation. Key endpoints of the trial include safety and tolerability, time to hypoglycemia during fasting, and changes from baseline in corn starch supplementation. In May 2025, we announced the dosing of the first patient in the trial.

Limitations of nuclease editing

Gene editing works by disrupting, inserting, or modifying genes in the natural context of the genome. Most established gene editing methods rely on a class of enzymes, called nucleases, to make a double-stranded break in the DNA at a targeted location. Nuclease editors have several significant limitations.

First, there is a lack of predictability in genetic outcomes when altering gene sequences with nucleases. Nuclease editors can be effective if the desired outcome is to knock out or switch off the whole gene, but do not allow for precise control of the specific genetic outcome at the target site and its effects may vary from individual to individual.
